claims.text: The initially solid Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles are homogeneous.
Thermally activated copper surface segregation governs the premelting and melting behavior of Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles.
Copper is the lower-melting-point component of the alloy.
Copper enrichment at the nanoparticle surface forms a liquid-like layer before bulk melting.
A copper-enriched surface layer lowers the nanoparticle's apparent melting point relative to a compositionally homogeneous particle.
Rapid quenching can lock in a homogeneous elemental distribution in these nanoparticles.
Thermal annealing promotes copper diffusion to and enrichment at the nanoparticle surface.
Copper has lower cohesive energy than the other relevant components of the nanoparticle.
Copper has sufficiently high diffusivity during heating to migrate to the nanoparticle surface.
Copper accumulation lowers the local melting temperature at the nanoparticle surface.
Surface premelting can occur while the nanoparticle core remains solid until a higher temperature.
Annealed nanoparticles with copper surface segregation will exhibit an earlier onset of surface premelting than rapidly quenched homogeneous nanoparticles.
Annealed nanoparticles with copper surface segregation will have a lower overall melting point than rapidly quenched homogeneous nanoparticles.
The proposed mechanism applies to Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles approximately 10–100 nm in size under controlled heating.
Different diffusion kinetics and thermodynamic driving forces may limit transfer of the hypothesis to larger particles or bulk samples.
